p: The word democracy is Greek, made of demos, the people, and kratos, power or rule. In my own century it is a word that frightens a good many respectable persons, who associate it with the mob of the French Revolution, and inspires a good many others, who associate it with the future. The Reform Act of eighteen sixty-seven, eight years ago, gave the vote to most male householders in the towns of England, and Mr Disraeli, who carried it, described it as a leap in the dark. The Athenians took that leap two thousand three hundred and eighty years ago. They did not land softly, but they landed.

Athens, in the sixth century before Christ, was a city of perhaps a few tens of thousands of citizens, ruled by its noble families, who quarrelled among themselves and oppressed the poor. A statesman named Solon, about five hundred and ninety-four years before Christ, cancelled the debts that had reduced many poor Athenians to slavery and gave every citizen a place in the assembly. Later the city fell under the rule of a tyrant, a word which to the Greeks meant simply a ruler who had seized power without lawful title, and was not necessarily a reproach; Peisistratus, who held the office, was by most accounts a capable one. His sons were less so. When they were driven out, a nobleman named Cleisthenes, in the year five hundred and eight before Christ, carried through a reform that broke the power of the old families by reorganising the citizens into ten new tribes, each mixed from different parts of the country, and gave supreme power to the assembly of all male citizens.

Athenian democracy was not like any government you or I have known. It was not representative: the citizens did not elect members to govern on their behalf. They governed themselves. The assembly, which any adult male citizen might attend, met some forty times a year on a hill called the Pnyx, and there, by a show of hands, decided war and peace, made laws, and voted on almost everything of importance. Any citizen might speak. A council of five hundred, chosen by lot from among the citizens, prepared the business. Most public offices were filled not by election but by lot, the Athenians believing that election favoured the rich and the eloquent, and that any citizen was capable of serving. The juries in the law courts were enormous, often five hundred or more, chosen by lot and paid a small wage so that the poor could serve. Only the generals, whose office required expert skill, were elected.

The Athenians had also a curious institution called ostracism. Once a year the assembly might vote whether to hold one, and if it did, each citizen scratched upon a fragment of broken pottery, called an ostrakon, the name of the man he thought most dangerous to the state. If enough votes were cast, the man with the most was banished for ten years, without loss of property or disgrace. Many of these potsherds have been found, some misspelt, some written in the same hand as though prepared in advance for illiterate voters, which suggests that the art of electioneering is also Greek.

We must not idealise it. The citizens were only the free men of Athenian birth. Women had no political rights at all. Resident foreigners, who were many, had none. And the slaves, who may have been a third of the population or more, had none, and their labour in the house, the workshop and the silver mines helped to give the citizens the leisure to govern. Athens was also, in the fifth century, an empire, which compelled the other Greek cities of its alliance to pay tribute, and punished those that revolted with great severity. The democracy that built the Parthenon on the Acropolis paid for it, in part, with the money of its subjects.

Nor was the democracy always wise. In four hundred and fifteen years before Christ, persuaded by the brilliant and unscrupulous Alcibiades, the assembly voted to send a great expedition to conquer Sicily, which ended in total disaster. Its long war with Sparta, described by Thucydides in the History of the Peloponnesian War, one of the greatest of all histories and one in whose cold intelligence every politician should be schooled, ended in defeat in four hundred and four. Yet the democracy recovered, and lasted, with interruptions, for nearly two hundred years: a longer life than many more admired constitutions.

It was the restored democracy which, in three hundred and ninety-nine years before Christ, put to death the most famous of its citizens. Socrates was a stonemason's son, ugly, poor and indefatigably curious, who spent his life in the streets and gymnasiums of Athens asking questions. He would ask a man who claimed to know what courage was, or justice, or piety, to define it, and then, by further questions, show him that his definition did not hold. The young men of the city loved to watch this; their fathers, often the victims of it, did not. Socrates wrote nothing. We know him chiefly through his pupil Plato, whose dialogues are the foundation of all Western philosophy, and through the soldier and historian Xenophon, and through a comedy by Aristophanes called The Clouds, which mocks him unmercifully.

He was accused of not believing in the gods of the city and of corrupting the young. Behind the charges lay politics: several of his associates, among them Alcibiades and Critias, had done Athens great harm. At his trial, as Plato reports it in the Apology, he declined to plead for mercy, said that the unexamined life is not worth living, and suggested that the appropriate penalty for his crimes would be free dinners at the public expense for life. He was condemned by a jury of five hundred and one, and died by drinking hemlock, discussing the immortality of the soul with his friends until the poison reached his heart.

The death of Socrates has troubled lovers of democracy ever since. Plato concluded that the people could not be trusted to govern, and wrote The Republic, in which philosophers rule. I draw a different moral. The Athenians killed one philosopher; most governments of the ancient world would not have let him speak at all. A democracy can do great wrong. But it is a democracy that leaves us the record of its own wrongs and the means to repent of them. The Athenians, it is said, soon regretted Socrates. Tyrants seldom regret anything.
